citations.quote:
Assume countable choice. Let $F_0,F_1\subset S^3$ be connected compact smooth spanning surfaces for the same nonempty link $L$. Suppose their interiors are transverse, their interior intersection $\Gamma$ is a finite disjoint union of embedded circles, and their interior boundary collars are disjoint in a neighborhood of $L$. A regular face is a connected component of $(\operatorname{int}F_i)\setminus\Gamma$. A complement region $R$ is a component of $S^3\setminus(F_0\cup F_1)$; it is incident to a regular face if its closure contains a point of that face.

Each individual complement $S^3\setminus F_i$ is path-connected. There are finitely many regular faces and complement regions, and each region is incident to a face of each surface. If a region $R$ is not incident to every regular face of both surfaces, then some circle $\gamma\subset\Gamma$ is two-sided in both surfaces and has this property: in a small normal disk at any point of $\gamma$, the sectors belonging to $R$ are exactly one of the four sectors cut by the two transverse surfaces, or exactly two adjacent sectors. In particular they are not two opposite sectors.

More generally, transporting the four sectors once around any common circle either fixes all sectors or exchanges each with its opposite. In the second case the circle is one-sided in both surfaces, and the sector set of any incident region is either an opposite pair or all four sectors.

Assume countable choice. Let $M$ be a compact connected smooth three-manifold with incoming and outgoing faces $A_0,A_1$, both nonempty, and vertical face $B\times[0,1]$, with supplied compatible product collars and boundary parametrizations. Neither the manifold nor its horizontal faces is required to be orientable or to have connected horizontal faces. Then there is an excellent Morse function $f:M\to[0,1]$ with $f^{-1}(i)=A_i$, equal to the prescribed height $t$ on a smaller full vertical product collar, with no boundary critical points, and with all its critical points of index one or two. All index-one values precede all index-two values.

More precisely, take the ordered relative handle presentation with no extrema supplied by the relative face handle lemma. The critical values can be any assigned finite strictly increasing list in $(0,1)$ in that handle order. Thus all index-one values may be assigned below $1/2$ and all index-two values above $1/2$. The resulting function retains the original boundary parametrizations and is product near every boundary face and corner.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

derivations.claim: Color a point of $S^3\setminus(F_0\cup F_1)$ by the parity of the total number of crossings with the surfaces along a generic path from one fixed complementary base point. This parity is path-independent. To verify it, join two such paths with reversed orientation and round their junctions off the surfaces. A smooth loop in $S^3$ misses some point: in finitely many charts its bounded-derivative image is covered by $N$ balls of radius $O(1/N)$, whose total three-dimensional volume tends to zero. Stereographic projection from a missed point puts the loop in $\mathbb R^3$; coning it to a point with a radial cutoff constant near the cone center gives a smooth spanning disk, retaining a constant collar of the boundary loop. Perturb its interior by [F3], fixing that collar, to be transverse to each surface interior and to $\Gamma$ and $L$. On the parameter disk the two surface preimages form a finite graph. At a preimage of $\Gamma$ it has valence four; at a preimage of $L$ it has two half-arcs, one from each spanning surface; every other interior vertex has valence two. Its boundary vertices are precisely the crossings of the loop, each of valence one. The finite graph degree sum makes their number even. This proves path-independence. Color is constant on each region and changes across each regular face. Hence at a common circle the dark sectors are two opposite quadrants, while at a boundary component they are either the quadrant between the two positive rays or its complementary three-quadrant sector.

Choose disjoint small normal tubes about the finitely many circles of $\Gamma$, away from the supplied boundary tubes. Their surface axes can be made exact in smooth fiber coordinates. In a normal disk over a circle point, parametrize the two surface curves as $c_0(s,u)$ and $c_1(s,v)$, vanishing at the center. Their independent tangent vectors make the fiber map $(u,v)\mapsto c_0(s,u)+c_1(s,v)$ a local diffeomorphism by [F4]. Shrinking uniformly makes it injective, and it carries the two coordinate axes to the actual surface curves. In the nontrivial case of [F1] its coordinate transitions around the circle are $(u,v)\mapsto(-u,-v)$; otherwise they are the identity, after choosing periodic frames. The dark pair is thus $uv>0$ or $uv<0$, unchanged by any simultaneous sign reversal. Blow up each circle of $\Gamma\cup L$ in these tubes by replacing the normal origin by its circle of polar directions. Explicitly retain $r\ge0$ and the normal angle, glue for $r>0$ to the punctured old tube and keep the same outer-radius collar. This produces a compact smooth three-manifold with torus boundary in place of the curves. It is Hausdorff by these compact bundle and unchanged-complement charts.

In this blown-up space take the closure $W_R$ of each dark region $R$. Along $\Gamma$ its two possible dark angular intervals are disjoint, so no opposite sectors are identified at their old central point. Along $L$ the chosen dark angular interval has length $\pi/2$ or $3\pi/2$, both strictly less than $2\pi$. Each closure is therefore a smooth compact connected three-manifold with product corners: its local charts are ordinary region charts, half-space charts at regular faces and polar product charts $(s,r,t)$ at the new boundary, where $t$ is the normalized angular interval coordinate. The two angular endpoints are respectively its incoming face from $F_0$ and outgoing face from $F_1$. Every $W_R$ has both horizontal faces nonempty by [F1]. Its vertical face is a finite union of circles times $[0,1]$. A vertical circle over a one-sided circle of $\Gamma$ may double-cover that base circle; the normalized angular coordinate is still a well-defined product height. All these are faces of the blown-up compact charts, not an assertion that the original closure of $R$ was a manifold at an opposite-sector crossing.

Fix the following angular heights near the vertical faces. At $\Gamma$, for dark pair $\eta uv>0$, where $\eta=\pm1$, use the interval whose rays are $(u,v)=(r\cos(\pi t/2),\eta r\sin(\pi t/2))$, with signed $r$ accounting for the two opposite sectors. On an individual blown-up sector take its nonnegative radius; the opposite sector has the same normalized $t$. At $L$ use $(u,v)=(r\cos(\alpha t),r\sin(\alpha t))$ for $r\ge0$, with $\alpha=\pi/2$ for the narrow dark sector and $\alpha=-3\pi/2$ for the wide one. These formulas run from the actual positive $F_0$ ray to the positive $F_1$ ray. The angular coordinate is compatible with the horizontal product corner coordinates. Apply [F2] to every $W_R$, using exactly these vertical height data. There are finitely many region pieces by [F1]. Assign their finitely many one-handle values distinct numbers below $1/2$ and all two-handle values distinct numbers above $1/2$, retaining each piece's handle order. The resulting height functions are exactly $t$ near their vertical faces.

Glue the vertical faces over each $\gamma\subset\Gamma$ by pairing opposite dark sectors at the same base point and the same normalized angle $t$. In the two-sided case this pairs two distinct boundary annuli, possibly on one region piece. In the one-sided case their single annulus double-covers $\gamma$ and is glued by its free deck involution. In both cases signed-radius charts give the smooth local model $(s,r,t)$ with $r\in\mathbb R$, including the transition $r\mapsto-r$ on going around a one-sided circle. The heights glue smoothly because they equal $t$ on full collars. Leave the vertical faces over $L$ unglued. The horizontal faces glue to the original smooth surfaces $F_0,F_1$, since the two signed radii restore their whole axis across every common circle. Call the resulting compact smooth face manifold $W$, its height $h$, and its blowdown projection to $S^3$ by $\pi$. Off the new vertical faces the projection is the original inclusion of a region or its regular boundary face.

Define $E(x)=(\pi(x),h(x))$. It is a smooth embedding. Off the new annuli the spatial projection is a local full-dimensional coordinate, so $dE$ has rank three. On an annulus over $\Gamma$ its formula is exactly $(s,r,t)\mapsto(s,r\cos(\pi t/2),\eta r\sin(\pi t/2),t)$ in the axis charts of step 2.1. Its differential has rank three even at $r=0$: the $s$ column is nonzero, the $r$ column is a unit vector in the normal disk, and the $t$ column has time entry one. The same computation holds at $L$ with $r\ge0$ and either value of $\alpha$ in step 4.1, giving its vertical boundary and horizontal corners. These formulas respect simultaneous sign monodromy. Distinct points with the same spatial projection can occur only on a glued annulus over $\Gamma$ or on an unglued one over $L$: every regular face has exactly one dark side, and region interiors are disjoint. On each such interval fiber the height is $t$, so $E$ is injective there as well. A smooth injective immersion from compact $W$ into the Hausdorff cylinder, with these corner charts, is an embedding; equivalently its continuous inverse follows from compactness and its local embedding charts. Its boundary is precisely the three faces asserted in the Statement.

Every region piece meets its incoming face, and the incoming surface $F_0$ is connected. Its regular faces are joined across the cut common circles, and the gluing in step 5.1 makes those same joins inside $W$. Thus every region piece is in the one component containing $F_0$, so $W$ is connected. The time function has exactly the critical points chosen inside the region pieces: the annulus models and all boundary collars have nonzero $t$ derivative. It is excellent with only the assigned index-one and index-two values, in the stated order. Finally replace $h$ by any $g$ as in the Statement. Away from the interval fibers the differential of $\pi$ is still invertible, while near the fibers the map is unchanged. Injectivity uses the same singleton-fiber and fixed-interval-height argument as step 6.1. The endpoint-fiber hypothesis retains the exact horizontal faces, while the unchanged collars retain the vertical face and corners. Compactness then gives another smooth embedding. This proves the asserted reheighting property precisely for this constructed projection, without a claim about arbitrary intrinsic Morse functions on arbitrary embedded cobordisms.

Step 7.1 handles zero or either type of critical point.

citations.quote: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). For every compact collared triad $(W;M_0,M_1)$ there are an adapted excellent Morse function $f:W\to[0,1]$ and an adapted complete downward gradient-like field $X$, both agreeing with the product model on smaller neighborhoods in the fixed collars: $f=t_0/3$ near $M_0$, $f=1-t_1/3$ near $M_1$, and $X$ is its negative Riemannian gradient for a metric that is a product metric there. Here **adapted complete** has the collar-extension meaning of [[def-morse-function-adapted-to-a-cobordism]]: $X$ is the restriction of a complete smooth field on a boundaryless collar extension of $W$; a trajectory is followed in $W$ only until it exits a face.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. On a compact collared triad $(W;M_0,M_1)$, every adapted excellent Morse function determines a finite handle decomposition relative to $M_0$, with one handle of index $\operatorname{ind}(p)$ per critical point. Given an adapted field, the attaching sphere is the boundary of its local unstable disk transported to the lower regular level. Conversely every finite handle decomposition relative to $M_0$ is realized by an adapted excellent Morse function with one critical point per handle, of the same index, ordered by the prescribed handle order.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(W;M_0,M_1)$ be a nonempty compact connected triad with
$M_0\ne\varnothing$ connected. Then $W$ admits a handle decomposition relative
to $M_0$ with no $0$-handles. If $M_0$ has $k$ components the same argument
leaves no $0$-handles and begins with $k-1$ connecting $1$-handles; if
$M_0=\varnothing$, exactly the $0$-handles needed to create the components of
$W$ remain, one per component.

derivations.claim: Regard $F$ as a two-dimensional collared triad with incoming face $\partial F$ and empty outgoing face, using [F1]. Its boundary is compact, so it has finitely many components: a finite cover by connected interval charts meets every component. The incoming face is nonempty and need not be connected. Apply [F2] and [F3] to obtain a finite relative presentation from $\partial F$ with no zero-handles. Since the dimension is two, every remaining handle has index one or two. The normalization in [F3] retains the incoming boundary identification.

Reverse this handle presentation. A $k$-handle $D^k\times D^{2-k}$ becomes a dual $(2-k)$-handle, by interchanging its attaching and outgoing faces and its two product factors. This follows directly in the handle product coordinates and their signed collar charts. Thus the reversed presentation starts from the empty face and uses only zero- and one-handles, with the same finite attaching and rounding data and with the actual boundary identification at its outgoing end. Order it with zero-handles first: the original normalization used index-ordered one- and two-handles, and reversing that order has exactly this effect.

In dimension two a zero-handle is a smooth disk. A one-handle $D^1\times D^1$ attaches along its two end intervals $S^0\times D^1$ and is precisely a rectangular band. The reversed presentation therefore is the claimed finite disk-and-band model. Its presentation diffeomorphism carries these finitely many pieces and their product collar charts onto $F$, including its outgoing boundary parametrization. No orientation was assumed by the Morse, tree-absorption or product-handle arguments, so twisted bands and nonorientable surfaces are included. At least one disk occurs because the surface is nonempty and the starting face is empty. This proves the geometric presentation assertion, not merely a deformation retraction to a graph.

citations.quote:
Assume countable choice. Let $F_0,F_1\subset S^3$ be connected compact smooth spanning surfaces for the same nonempty link $L$, whose transverse interior intersection $\Gamma$ is a finite disjoint union of circles. Supply disjoint boundary tubes with smooth coordinates $(s,u,v)$, with $L=\{u=v=0\}$, in which their actual boundary collars are $F_0=\{v=0,u\ge0\}$ and $F_1=\{u=0,v\ge0\}$. The surfaces need not be orientable.

There is a compact connected smooth three-manifold $W$ with product corners and an embedding $E:W\hookrightarrow S^3\times[0,1]$ with horizontal faces $A_0,A_1$ mapped exactly to $F_0\times\{0\}$ and $F_1\times\{1\}$, and with vertical boundary mapped exactly to $L\times[0,1]$. Its ambient time function is excellent Morse, with only index-one and index-two interior critical points, all index-one values below $1/2$ and all index-two values above $1/2$. It is the product height near every boundary face and near the interior annuli above $\Gamma$.

The spatial projection $\pi=\operatorname{pr}_{S^3}\circ E$ has one-point fibers wherever its image is outside $\Gamma\cup L$, and its fiber over each point of $\Gamma\cup L$ is exactly an interval. More precisely, if $g:W\to[0,1]$ is any smooth function agreeing with the original time on neighborhoods of those interval fibers and on horizontal collars, and $g^{-1}(i)=A_i$ for $i=0,1$, then $x\mapsto(\pi(x),g(x))$ is again a smooth embedding with the same boundary data. This last assertion is restricted to these explicit projection fibers, rather than to arbitrary embedded cobordisms.

Let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth, let $p$ be a nondegenerate critical point of
$f$, and let $\lambda$ be the index of $p$. If $n=\dim M$, then there are local
coordinates $(x^1,\dots,x^n)$ centered at $p$ in which

$$f=f(p)-\sum_{i=1}^{\lambda}(x^i)^2+\sum_{i=\lambda+1}^{n}(x^i)^2.$$

For $n=0$, both sums are empty.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. In a sufficiently small Morse chart $f=c-|u|^2+|v|^2$, with $u\in\mathbb R^k$ and $v\in\mathbb R^{n-k}$, the change across $c$ is a rounded index-$k$ handle: a compact product piece attaches along $S^{k-1}\times D^{n-k}$ on $f=c-\varepsilon$, its core is $v=0$, and after a local modification the remaining region up to $c+\varepsilon$ is a regular collar. The modification agrees with $f$ off a compact subset of the chart. The collar assertion is made inside a compact band having no other critical point.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$. For each $p\in M$, let
$\gamma_p:I_p\to M$ be the maximal integral curve through $p$, and set

$$ \mathcal D:=\{(t,p)\in\mathbb R\times M:t\in I_p\}, \qquad \Phi(t,p):=\gamma_p(t). $$

Then $\mathcal D$ is open in $\mathbb R\times M$, each fibre $\mathcal D_p$ is
an interval containing $0$, the map $\Phi:\mathcal D\to M$ is smooth, and
$\Phi$ is the unique maximal local flow generated by $X$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Assume countable choice. Every connected compact smooth surface $F$ with nonempty boundary has a finite smooth disk-and-band presentation: it is diffeomorphic, respecting its actual boundary parametrization, to finitely many smooth disks with finitely many rectangular bands attached along pairs of disjoint boundary intervals, with compatible corner rounding. Equivalently it has a finite handle decomposition with only zero- and one-handles, all zero-handles first. The assertion allows nonorientable surfaces and twisted bands. For a smoothly embedded surface these data may be transported to the actual surface, so its disk, band and attaching charts are supplied inside that surface, rather than merely as a homotopy type.

derivations.claim: Take the actual embedded cobordism $E:W\to S^3\times[0,1]$ in [F1], and write its time function as $h$. For a regular $t$, the level $W_t$ is a compact smooth surface with boundary its intersection with the vertical face. Its spatial projection is an embedding: on tangent vectors of $W_t$, $dh=0$, so a vector killed by spatial projection is killed by $dE$ and must vanish; injectivity follows from that of $E$ at the common time. Its image $F_t\subset S^3$ has boundary exactly $L$. The endpoint collars give the initial and final surfaces in the same way. There are finitely many distinct critical heights.

At a critical point the spatial differential on $W$ is invertible: the time differential vanishes there and $E$ is an immersion of dimension three. By [F3] the cobordism near that point is a graph $t=f(x,y,z)$ on a spatial chart, and [F2] gives its quadratic normal form. For index one write $f=c-x^2+|y|^2$, with $y\in\mathbb R^2$. Choose the local lowering cutoff and a small $\varepsilon$ as in [F2], then choose its sufficiently small positive $d$. Its actual lower level contains the two end disks of the embedded product $H_0=\{|y|^2\le d,\ x^2\le\varepsilon+|y|^2\},\qquad (U,V)\longmapsto(\sqrt{\varepsilon+d|V|^2}\,U,\sqrt d\,V)$, where $(U,V)\in D^1\times D^2$. The end disks $U=\pm1$ lie on $f=c-\varepsilon$, and the product interior misses that level. The lateral face is its attaching tube. Rounding its seams with the retained lower level gives the boundary graph $|y|^2=j(x^2)$ of the explicit local construction in [F2]. The graph interpolation there is an ambient isotopy supported in this spatial chart and carries that rounded tube replacement to the lower level of the locally lowered function. The spatial chart lies in one region interior of [F1], so no other part of the surface projects into it. Thus this is an actual embedded product-cylinder tube addition in $S^3$, with the rest of the surface retained.

On a compact band without critical points choose a smooth field $X$ on $W$ with $dh(X)=1$, tangent to the vertical boundary and equal to its product $\partial_t$ near that boundary. One obtains it by dividing coordinate fields by their nonzero height derivative and patching finitely many local choices; their convex combination still has $dh(X)=1$. Uniqueness in [F3] prevents a trajectory from crossing the boundary face to which the field is tangent. A finite cover of the compact band gives a common short existence time, and restarting its local flows finitely often transports the lower level to every intervening level, since its height increases at unit speed. Projection of that transport gives an isotopy of compact surfaces in $S^3$ by step 1.1. On the vertical boundary the projection is the fixed point of $L$, so [F4] extends it to an ambient isotopy fixing $L$ pointwise. This proves the required assertion for every regular band, including those later used with a locally modified height.

Choose the lowering cutoff and $\varepsilon$ so small that its support is disjoint from the fixed interval fibers and all boundary collars, its modified height stays in $(0,1)$ there, and the chosen band contains no other critical point. Its upper sublevel, hence its upper regular level, is unchanged by the local lowering construction in [F2]. The new band from the modified lower level to that upper level is regular. The reheighting assertion of [F1] verifies that this modified height still gives an embedded cobordism; step 2.2 therefore gives an ambient isotopy from the tube-replacement surface to the original upper level. This verifies the geometric comparison, rather than inferring it from an abstract handle diffeomorphism. For index two reverse time and use the same index-one construction; its change is a tube removal. In both cases every modification and graph isotopy is away from $L$. Applying this at the finitely many critical heights and step 2.2 between them gives the finite sequence with all additions before all removals.

Every surface in that sequence is connected. Before the first critical value the level is isotopic to connected $F_0$. A tube addition to one connected surface cannot disconnect it, so all levels through the index-one phase stay connected. During the index-two phase a tube removal is compression along a single circle; it either retains the component count or increases it, and never joins distinct components. No zero- or three-handle occurs, so there is no later sphere birth or death to change this conclusion. Since the final surface $F_1$ is connected, no removal can increase the component count. Consequently all regular levels, and all tube-replacement and ambient-isotopic representatives constructed above, remain connected. Their boundary is $L$ throughout.

Apply [F5] to each of the finitely many connected compact boundary surfaces in this sequence to supply its actual finite smooth presentation. The isotopies fix every point of $L$, and each local cylinder is disjoint from it, so any boundary component orientation or label is retained. The index order from [F1] and the constructions in step 3.1 give the claimed order of the finite moves, completing the assertion without assuming orientability.
